p: Wes's truck was in the lot at ten to seven on Friday, parked inside the lines for once. Half the high bay lights were still on night mode. She found him inside HEARTH at the relief plate by the hatch, cargo drawings rolled under one arm, pencil behind his ear, same shirt as yesterday.

He didn't say good morning. I went through all eleven cargo sets, he said. Every place a manual valve sits in front of something that's supposed to work by itself. There's one more. The cabin pressure transducers. Same valve, same tag, so we could leak test the port. He flicked the red handle with a fingernail. It didn't move. Twenty years I've been putting these in.
He'd drawn the fix in pencil on the back of a cargo drawing. The red valve was gone. The two relief valves bolted straight onto the tee, and the tee onto the one fitting through the shell.
Cargo had one hole, and I'm keeping it, he said. I'm losing the handle.
Tiago pulls both valves and plugs the ports. Proof, leak, then the valves go back on and get their own leak check in place.
And the night somebody leaves a plug in.
She heard it as it came out. Three weeks back, at Callie's sink, dish towel in hand, she'd said it nearly word for word, and Callie had dropped the towel on the counter.

Wes didn't argue. Tiago did. He'd come in early too, and was leaning in the hatch with a coffee from the gas station on Arapahoe. Then the plug's got a handle on it as long as my forearm, painted red, he said. Make it so the vent cap won't go on with a plug in. You can't close the plate over one. Wes looked at him, then wrote it on the drawing.
It was Callie's answer with a wrench in it. Build it so the crew won't let him up. Nadia kept that to herself.

Odette came up at nine and rewrote HR-22 at the HEARTH room table. The two relief valves would share only the tee and the fitting through the shell, passive metal, covered the way the shell itself was covered: design for minimum risk, big margins, proved at proof pressure with everything else. The plugs went on the closeout list as ground items. Two people would sign that both were out before the plate closed for flight.
Two valves, two plugs, two names, she said, and wrote that across the bottom of the page.

The product baseline had been under the board since CDR, so the fix would go in as a change request. Wes wrote it himself, with the transducer valve on the same page, and put his own name in the box for the requester. Then he rolled the cargo drawings up and tucked them back under his arm.
It was one valve, he said.

Monday of week twenty five Tiago's integration sequence covered most of the wall in his office off the high bay: twenty one steps, from the first breaker in HEARTH's power distribution to the rack making air. The stand-in had been in its bay since Thursday, its steel ballast built to the ICD's number with Tamarack's connectors on its back.
The real rack would reach the high bay in week twenty six and go into HEARTH in week twenty seven. Proof testing started in week twenty nine.

Two weeks of steps on a steel box, Amara said. Then we do them again on the real one. Tell me why I'm paying twice. Wes, from the doorway: Put the rack in first when it gets here. It's the one that's late. Build around it.

The twenty one steps fall into four stages, and each stage ends with a check before the next one starts. The stand-in holds the rack's place through the first three. For the data stage Jun writes a simulator that answers on HEARTH's network the way the rack's controller will. Nothing that can be proven on the steel box waits for the real one. It gets proven early, where a fault can only be in the last thing added. Amara takes back four days by running checkouts on a second shift.

Tuesday the harness shop's lead caught Nadia at the shop door with a spool in each hand. The stand-in's harnesses had come off his pegboards in week twenty three, built from the shop's cargo stock, which was fine for a steel box that would never leave the ground. Now he was building the flight set, and the wire the drawings called for had run out four harnesses short.
The supplier quoted five weeks. On his shelf sat two thousand meters of cargo wire, same gauge, same color code. He held that spool up.
It's flown, he said. I can have the set done Friday.

Jun has the answer by lunch. HEARTH's cabin wire has to pass the crewed cabin flammability and offgassing tests, and the cargo wire's insulation was never tested to that standard. Cargo modules weren't built for people to live in. The harness lead calls distributors while Jun finds an equal on the approved list. A warehouse in Aurora has eight hundred meters of it, three days out. The shop builds those four last, and each traveler says which reel.

The board approved Wes's change on Tuesday. Wednesday morning Gus cut the safety wire and lifted the red valve out of the relief line, and Wes asked for it. It went on the shelf over his desk with its tag still on. Jun took a kilogram and a half off the mass roll-up. Every kilogram counted now, on a margin of about 810.

Amara wanted the relief tee written up as a lesson learned before the week was out. FRO's lessons learned lived in a shared folder: two hundred and fourteen documents, the newest eight years old. Tiago said he'd opened it once, to see if it existed.

Lessons learned is where a lesson goes to die, Wes said. I've got thirty years of these, and they're up here. He tapped his temple with the pencil. If a second module ever came, Osprey's or anyone's, it would start from HEARTH's drawings.

It goes where the next designer will trip on it. FRO's design review checklist gets a line: no single manual valve, plug or cap in the path of controls meant to work alone. The standard relief drawing loses its valve. The lesson gets one paragraph with the cargo history, the fix, Odette's name and Wes's. Then Jun asks Wes for an hour a week to walk the cargo drawings with a recorder running. Wes says two hours, and bring coffee.

Thursday Tiago walked Nadia and FRO's facilities manager through the pressure test cell. HEARTH's proof test was set for week twenty nine. The cell had been built for cargo modules, and the facilities manager had kept it running since the first one.

Tiago had his list on a clipboard. The nitrogen line into the cell was sized for a cargo module, and HEARTH's ninety cubic meters would take fourteen hours to fill. The cell's pressure gauges came due for calibration in week thirty, and the calibration lab was booked three weeks out. The compressor's yearly service sat on the facilities calendar in week twenty nine. A second module, if one came, would want the same cell the year after.
It's run fine for eleven modules, the facilities manager said. Tell me what's different.

Tiago's clipboard turns into a page: what HEARTH needs from the cell, week by week, through ship. The compressor service moves to week twenty six. The gauges go to the calibration lab in week twenty seven, good through ship, not just through proof. A bigger nitrogen line goes on the facilities plan for the winter shutdown, with a trailer to cover HEARTH until then. The facilities manager adds the cell to the page he shows FRO's board every quarter, with HEARTH's dates and a blank row for the next module.

Sunday at eight she'd made her call to Pueblo and kept it to the weather. Callie had put a photo in the family thread that afternoon, no caption: the first red tomato off the plants out back, held up in both of Rosie's hands. Nadia typed three replies, deleted them, and sent a heart.

Monday the flight harnesses started coming off the shop's pegboards. Each label carried a drawing number and a dash: dash one for the stand-in set built in week twenty three, dash three for flight. The rack's power harness was W-114. Its data harness was W-117. On the cargo modules the shop had tested harnesses after they were installed, all of them in one day.
Saves a day on the bench, the harness lead said. We've always done it that way.

Every wire gets continuity and insulation resistance on the bench, where a fault costs a re-crimp instead of a day inside the module. Each harness leaves with a traveler: drawing, dash number, serial, wire reel, crimp tool, the tester's name, and the numbers. Jun asks the shop to wrap the stand-in's dash ones in yellow tape at both ends, so they can't be mistaken for flight.

The rack came down from Frederick on Tuesday of week twenty six in a box truck, and Irena rode in the cab with her own torque wrench on her lap. She'd built most of its frame. Her week at the lake started the Thursday after first power.

It sat in the high bay on its dolly under a clean tent. Tiago had the install for Monday and first power for Tuesday. The stand-in had carried Tamarack's own connectors since week twenty four, and every one of them had mated.
Connectors fit, Tiago said. Do I need more than that?

Jun builds the checklist from the ICD, line by line. Every pin at HEARTH's harness ends. Voltage at the connector with a load on it. The rack's chassis bond to its mounts. Coolant pressure and flow at the quick disconnects, with water at temperature. On the rack's side, its connector pinouts against the same pages. Everything checks. One question goes on the open list: the ICD says how the rack's chassis bonds to HEARTH, and nothing about where the data cable's shield is grounded.

Friday FRO's flight software lead brought HEARTH's half of the rack software to Tiago's integration meeting. Her team had been working in sprints since week twelve. The newest build on her branch had a fix in it from Wednesday, for a command signing timeout they'd hit in the lab.
I'll load whatever's newest Tuesday morning, she said. Every day it's better.

Version 0.9.2 is tagged Friday afternoon with Wednesday's fix in it, and released to integration the controlled way: a named version, approved, with a record of what's in it. Four hundred and twelve unit tests, all passing. Three known issues, each with a workaround, on one page. The integration log records the version and the file's checksum. On Tuesday, when the panel says 0.9.2, everyone in the bay knows exactly what that is.

Monday of week twenty seven the real rack went into its bay. By noon HEARTH's integration had produced a binder of as-run procedures in Tiago's pencil, three hundred photos on Gus's phone, and the model check results on Jun's laptop.
Irena had brought Tamarack's acceptance data on a thumb drive, every page stamped proprietary.
At two Helen called. Halo wanted to see HEARTH's integration data as it came in, and Halo's sustaining engineers would need it for fifteen years after that.

Jun and Tiago set up the integration record that afternoon. Every as-run procedure, photo and anomaly report gets an ID, a date, and the configuration it was taken on. Gus's photos go in named by step. Halo gets a view of everything FRO owns. Tamarack's pages stay marked, visible only to the people Pavel's agreement names. The plan says who keeps it, in what format, and for how long: fifteen years, then the station's end of life.

Tuesday evening, with the rack mated, Tiago stood at the power panel with the procedure clipped open. W-114 ran the rack's power down from the overhead channel. W-117 ran its data. Both were dash three, flight, off the shop's bench the week before. Irena stood at the rack's front face, where the controller's screen would come up.
The stand-in's been powered forty times, Tiago said. How careful do you want this?

The power card comes up at ten percent current limit, then half, then full. The controller boots. The fans go to low speed, then high. At every hold Jun reads the numbers against the band he predicted, and each one sits inside it. At twenty to nine the rack is pulling cabin air through its sorbent beds in its own bay. Tiago writes the time on the procedure's last page.
Tiago had been running two shifts since the rack went in. When first shift came on Wednesday, second shift had left a page on the clipboard.

Integration anomaly report IAR-27-03, HEARTH rack bay (open). Observed: rack controller drops off HEARTH's network. Nine times in fourteen hours, four to six seconds each.. Pattern: every drop within two seconds of the rack fans stepping up to high speed.. Configuration: real rack. W-114 dash 3, power. W-117 dash 3, data. Flight software 0.9.2.. Effect: CO2 removal pauses during each drop. Rack recovers on its own.. Status: open.
Gus already had a spare harness over his shoulder. Start swapping? he asked.

Tiago puts the rack in standby. Jun photographs every connector and writes each harness into the report by dash number and serial. On the whiteboard they list what could cause it: power noise, the data harness, the controller, the software. Jun turns that into a numbered plan, one change per step, each with what it should show and how to put it back. Gus initials each step as he does it. By four the drops follow fan speed and nothing else. Jun pulls both drawings. Tamarack grounds the data cable's shield at the rack. HEARTH's drawing grounds it at both ends. Two grounds and a fan motor make a loop.

Wednesday night second shift put the stand-in's data harness into the rack bay, W-117 dash one, from the week twenty three set. It grounded the shield at HEARTH's end only, the old cargo way. It was step six on Jun's plan.

By Thursday morning the rack had run eleven hours with its fans on high and hadn't dropped once. Irena had seen it as soon as Jun showed her HEARTH's drawing. Tamarack had always grounded its shields at the rack. She'd pushed her lake week back two days to watch the night run, and didn't mention it.
It works, Tiago said. Proof test's in two weeks. Leave it in, and make the drawing match.

By noon the as-built list says W-117 dash one is installed, temporary, with a red tag on the harness itself. A change request grounds the shield at HEARTH's end only, on the drawing and in a new ICD revision that finally says how both sides handle shields. The board approves it Friday. The shop builds W-117 dash five on Monday from flight wire, it goes in Tuesday, and the list changes again that afternoon.

Monday of week twenty eight Odette needed one thing before she'd sign HEARTH into the proof test: that the module in the cell would be the module on the drawings. Ines came up from quality to ask the same question her own way.
Brannock's fifteen year aging result on the long cure lot was due Friday.
What's in it? Ines asked. Not what's on the list. What's in it.

Jun and Ines plan it for Monday of week twenty nine, the day before proof: every item on the as-built list found in the module, its label and serial read, its drawing and revision checked. Ines wants two people on each check and no one checking their own work. A functional audit against the requirements goes on the plan for the end of testing.

Friday of week twenty eight Gus was putting the troubleshooting kit back in the cage. Nadia was at Tiago's desk with the proof test procedure, her phone face down beside it, because Brannock's result was due by five.

Gus came out of the cage with a harness coiled in a clear bag, its traveler folded inside. He set it on the desk between the procedure and her phone. Nadia turned the bag until the label came around. W-114, dash three. Serial seven.
Pulled it myself, Gus said. Wednesday, end of my shift. I was going to put it back first thing.

Power had been the first branch on the whiteboard. He'd put in the stand-in's harness to rule it out, nothing changed, and he'd bagged the flight one so it wouldn't get stepped on. That night the drops stopped, and there was never a next step. It was on Jun's plan in Gus's initials. Step four: W-114 to dash one, no change. Step five: restore W-114. Step five had nothing beside it. Step six had second shift's initials. Jun's drawings had pointed at the shield by four, and second shift had gone straight to it.

Nadia opened the as-built list on her laptop. W-114, dash three, serial seven, installed week twenty seven. It said exactly what should have been there. W-117 had changed twice in a week, and both changes were on the list. W-114 had never been changed on purpose, so it had never been changed at all.

In the rack bay, under the overhead channel's cover, the rack's power ran through a dash one: built in week twenty three for a steel box of ballast, out of cargo wire. Nadia had turned that wire away herself in week twenty five, for a crewed cabin. It had yellow tape at both ends. Second shift had worked beside it Tuesday putting in dash five, and nobody looks twice at a harness that isn't the problem.
It's run clean all week, Tiago said.
On that. Ines's walk-down was Monday. It would have turned up then.

The night somebody leaves a plug in. She'd said it at Callie's sink. It hadn't been a plug, and the man who'd left it was the one who carried it out of the cage. Callie would have something to say about that. Nadia didn't know yet what she'd say back.
Gus looked back at the cage. There was a seal in a bag on that shelf for two years once, he said. This one's been nine days.
